A hacker may try to justify gaining unauthorized access to unsecured data by reasoning that because the data are not protected, anyone should be able to read it. But by analogy, someone who finds the front door of a house unlocked is not justified in entering the house and snooping around. Entering an unlocked house is trespassing, and trespassing violates the privacy of the house’s occupants [2].

A software tester neglects to sufficiently test a new module for a telephone switching system, and the module fails. Although the subsequent telephone service outages are not intended, the software tester is morally responsible for the harms caused by the outages [3].

A hacker installs a keystroke logging program in a deliberate attempt to steal passwords at a public computer. Even if the program fails to work, the hacker is still morally responsible for attempting to invade the privacy of users [3].

A hardware engineer might notice a design flaw that could result in a severe electrical shock to someone who opens a personal computer system unit to replace a memory chip. Even if the engineer is not specifically assigned to check the electrical safety of the system unit, the engineer is morally responsible for calling attention to the design flaw, and the engineer can be held accountable for failing to act [3].

The designer of a search engine for an online retailer might choose to display the most expensive items first. This choice might favor the interest of the retailer, to maximize profit, over the interest of the customer, to minimize cost [5].

results.q: What is the difference between moral responsibility and legal resnposibility. Give example.
results.answer: Moral responsibility tends to be shared among many individuals, whereas causal, role, and legal responsibilities tend to be exclusive [1]. Legal responsibility involves being charged with a crime or being liable for damages in a civil lawsuit, such as a physician being sued for malpractice or a manufacturer being found liable under strict liability even if the product met safety standards [3]. An example of moral responsibility is when a software tester is held responsible for harms caused by outages despite not intending them, or when a hacker is responsible for attempting to invade privacy even if their program fails [2]. An example of legal responsibility is when AECL could have been sued in the Therac-25 case for damages resulting from the radiation treatment machine [3].
